newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia says will not release papers to The Hague.
newsitem.headline: Croatia says will not release papers to The Hague.

text.p: Croatia said on Monday it would fight demands to release documents that could be used as evidence against a Bosnian Croat general who is being tried at an international tribunal in The Hague.

The tribunal told Croatia on Saturday it had four weeks to provide information about Tihomir Blaskic, renewing a request first made six months ago, and rebuffed Croatia's claims that it was not entitled to demand the evidence.
It said that, if Croatia did not hand over the files, Defence Minister Gojko Susak would be summoned to court to explain why.

"We will use all legal means available...all measures that we can to protect our right as a sovereign state and our right not to present documents deemed to be of national interest," Deputy Prime Minister Ljerka Mintas-Hodak told a news conference.
She said such documents must not be allowed into the public domain in the court.

"This decision represents a very dangerous precedent for all states. It is not only inconvenient for Croatia, because any other state can face the same situation. We will use all means available to clarify the question," Mintas-Hodak said.

Croatia has cited national security reasons for not complying with the six-month-old subpoena, which runs out on August 18. It also says that an individual, in this case Susak, is not bound to comply with the court's demands as these can only be addressed to a government.

However the court said in a statement any objection to an order to produce documents, "including a claim that a State's national security interests could be threatened by disclosure, does not automatically excuse the State or individual from compliance".

Sources say the documents include Blaskic's notes to the Croatian Defence Ministry, its records on arms supplies to Bosnian Croats and orders he received from the head of the separatist Bosnian Croat entity.
The subpoena called on Croatia to hand over 13 categories of documents relating to Blaskic's case.
Blaskic, aged 36, is accused of directing a brutal ethnic cleansing campaign against Bosnian Moslems in 1993, when he was commander of the Bosnian Croat militia in Central Bosnia.

Charges include killing and wounding women, children and the elderly in their homes and detaining Bosnian Moslem civilians. These people were forced to dig trenches, used as human shields, intimidated, abused and some ultimately beaten or shot to death, the indictments say.

The court said in reponse to Croatia's complaints that it had examined the relevant statutes and rules and decided it was not "attributing criminal responsibility" to Croatia, but was "merely exercising its necessary incidental judicial functions" to fulfil its purpose.

Croatia has been under strong international pressure to do more to comply with the tribunal and the United States has already blocked two loans because it was not satisfied with Crotia's progress. President Franjo Tudjman told Reuters earlier this month that Croatia was "prepared to cooperate with The Hague".
